name: Liability When Agents Interact
title: Liability When Agents Interact
answer: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents interact without a human directly approving each step. It includes agent-to-agent contracts, automated negotiations, shared task execution, and harm that spreads across systems operated by different parties. The focus is on how existing doctrines of agency, contract, tort, and product liability apply when no single human actor can be identified as the decision maker. It also tracks how courts and regulators are beginning to treat multi-agent chains as a distinct source of legal risk.

crumbs.name: Knowledge Based Professions and their Future

sections.body: This page covers legal responsibility when two or more AI agents interact without a human directly approving each step. It includes agent-to-agent contracts, automated negotiations, shared task execution, and harm that spreads across systems operated by different parties. The focus is on how existing doctrines of agency, contract, tort, and product liability apply when no single human actor can be identified as the decision maker. It also tracks how courts and regulators are beginning to treat multi-agent chains as a distinct source of legal risk.
sections.heading: Scope

sections.body: Liability analysis depends on the technical infrastructure that records what each agent did. Persistent logs, agent identity registries, model version records, and communication protocols provide the evidence base for assigning responsibility. Smart contract platforms and secure messaging layers can create immutable records of agent commitments, but they do not by themselves resolve legal questions. The practical infrastructure also includes monitoring systems, human override mechanisms, and audit trails that show when a person reviewed or approved an agent action.
sections.heading: What it runs on

sections.body: Lawyers and courts work by tracing the causal chain from an agent's output back to design choices, training data, deployment settings, and human oversight points. They apply familiar tests from agency law to ask whether an agent acted with apparent authority, and from product liability to ask whether the system was defective or unreasonably dangerous. Contract formation is examined through offer, acceptance, and intent, often by looking at the agent's programming and the principal's terms of use. Negligence analysis focuses on whether the operator failed to monitor, constrain, or test the agent before letting it interact with others.
sections.heading: How the work is done

sections.body: Rights and risks turn on provenance: who built the agent, who deployed it, what data and models it used, and who stood to benefit from its actions. Data provenance and model provenance records help establish whether a harmful interaction stemmed from a known flaw, a third-party component, or an unexpected emergent behavior. Risk is typically allocated through contracts, indemnification clauses, insurance policies, and platform terms of service, but these arrangements often lag behind the speed of agent-to-agent transactions. Privacy and intellectual property rights can be implicated when agents exchange personal data or reproduce protected material during interaction.
sections.heading: Rights, risk and provenance

sections.body: The direction of travel is toward clearer default rules for agent identity, mandatory logging, and minimum technical standards for autonomous interaction. Regulators are exploring registration schemes, agent-specific disclosure duties, and insurance or bonding requirements for high-risk deployments. Courts are likely to develop presumptions about human oversight and to refine the line between tool and principal as agents gain more independence. Cross-border coordination will matter because interacting agents often operate under different legal systems, and uniform technical standards may become a precondition for enforceable liability.
